questions.context:
Nucleophilic Substitution reaction of haloalkane can be conducted according to both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) mechanisms. \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) is a two step reaction while \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) is a single step reaction. For any haloalkane which mechanism is followed depends on factors such as structure of haloalkane, properties of leaving group, nucleophilic reagent and solvent.
Influences of solvent polarity : In \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction, the polarity of the system increases from the reactant to the transition state, because a polar solvent has a greater effect on the transition state than the reactant, thereby reducing activation energy and accelerating the reaction. In \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, the polarity of the system generally does not change from the reactant to the transition state and only charge dispersion occurs. At this time, polar solvent has a great stabilizing effect on Nu than the transition state, thereby increasing activation energy and slow down the reaction rate. For example, the decomposition rate \((\mathrm{S_N}1)\) of tertiary chlorobutane at 25 °C in water (dielectric constant 79) is 300000 times faster than in ethanol (dielectric constant 24). The reaction rate \((\mathrm{S_N}2)\) of 2-Bromopropane and NaOH in ethanol containing 40% water is twice slower than in absolute ethanol. Hence the level of solvent polarity has influence on both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, but with different results. Generally speaking weak polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, while strong polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}1\). Generally speaking the substitution reaction of tertiary haloalkane is based on \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) mechanism in solvents with a strong polarity (for example ethanol containing water).

questions.context:
Nucleophilic Substitution reaction of haloalkane can be conducted according to both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) mechanisms. \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) is a two step reaction while \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) is a single step reaction. For any haloalkane which mechanism is followed depends on factors such as structure of haloalkane, properties of leaving group, nucleophilic reagent and solvent.
Influences of solvent polarity : In \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction, the polarity of the system increases from the reactant to the transition state, because a polar solvent has a greater effect on the transition state than the reactant, thereby reducing activation energy and accelerating the reaction. In \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, the polarity of the system generally does not change from the reactant to the transition state and only charge dispersion occurs. At this time, polar solvent has a great stabilizing effect on Nu than the transition state, thereby increasing activation energy and slow down the reaction rate. For example, the decomposition rate \((\mathrm{S_N}1)\) of tertiary chlorobutane at 25 °C in water (dielectric constant 79) is 300000 times faster than in ethanol (dielectric constant 24). The reaction rate \((\mathrm{S_N}2)\) of 2-Bromopropane and NaOH in ethanol containing 40% water is twice slower than in absolute ethanol. Hence the level of solvent polarity has influence on both \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) and \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, but with different results. Generally speaking weak polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction, while strong polar solvent is favourable for \(\mathrm{S_N}1\). Generally speaking the substitution reaction of tertiary haloalkane is based on \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) mechanism in solvents with a strong polarity (for example ethanol containing water).
